newsitem.title: ITALY: Vatican, Jewish group slam cemetery desecration.
newsitem.headline: Vatican, Jewish group slam cemetery desecration.

text.p: The Vatican on Monday condemned a desecration of Jewish graves in Rome, calling it "an offence against history", while Jewish leaders said they were worried about growing anti-semitism in Italy.
Vandals attacked the graves early on Sunday, breaking tombstones and ripping the names and Stars of David off several others. Jewish leaders blamed the attack on skinheads.
Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro Valls blasted the attack. "This is an offence to the memory of the dead and an offence to history," he told reporters.

One tomb was surrounded with barbed wire and swastikas with the words "Arbeit macht frei" (work brings freedom), the slogan at the entrance to the Auschwitz death camp in Poland where millions of Jews died during World War Two.

Shimon Samuels, director for international affairs for the Simon Wiesenthal Centre, a Paris-based Jewish rights group, said he believed an organised neo-Nazi group with international contacts had carried out the attack.
"What starts at a cemetery ends with the living," Samuels told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"We are expecting a forthright reaction from the Italian authorities to ban this group which has strong international connections," Samuels added.
Judicial sources said Rome magistrates were investigating the possible involvement in the attack of rightwing racist sympathisers linked to a group known as the "Western Political Movement".
Senate speaker Nicola Mancino on Monday called the desecration "barbaric" in a letter to the head of Italy's Jewish community, Tullia Zevi.
Samuels said he was worried the unresolved war crimes case of former SS captain Erich Priebke could help provoke skinheads sympathetic to his cause to increase their anti-semitic acts.
"The longer this case is unresolved, the more likely it is that measures against the dead will escalate into atrocities against the living," Samuels said.
Priebke is in jail pending a decision by Italy's highest court on how to proceed in a new war crimes trial against him.

A first trial ended in uproar in August when a court found him guilty for his role in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity but not liable for punishment. The high court must now decide if a military or civilian court should hold the new trial.
